title: Where Do Demons Come From?
bigQuestion: Where did ancient Jewish and Christian readers think unclean spirits came from, and how did Heiser connect the answer to 1 Enoch?

story.title: The Man Who Ran to the Shore
story.kicker: On the far side of the Sea of Galilee, a man who has lived alone for a long time runs toward a boat.
paragraphs: The Gospel of Mark tells of a boat crossing the Sea of Galilee at night. Jesus and his followers land on the eastern shore, in the country of the Gerasenes. Most people there were not Jewish. On the hillside above the water, a large herd of pigs is feeding.

Near the shore are tombs cut into the rock. Mark says a man lived there, away from his town. People had tried to hold him with chains, but he broke them. Day and night he cried out among the tombs and the hills. The people of his town had stopped coming near.

Then Mark adds a surprising detail. When the man sees Jesus from far off, he does not run away. He runs toward him and kneels. Mark says an unclean spirit was troubling the man. Jesus speaks to it and asks its name. It answers, Legion, for we are many.

By the end of the story, the man is sitting calmly, dressed, next to Jesus. He asks to get into the boat and go along. Jesus says no. He tells him to go home to his own people and tell them what the Lord has done for him. The man goes through the Ten Cities, telling his story.

Readers have asked many questions about stories like this one. What did people in Jesus's time think these spirits were? Where did they come from? Michael Heiser gave one answer, drawn from an ancient book called 1 Enoch. This chapter looks at his answer, at other answers, and at how to read these stories with care.
story.think: The story ends with the man going home to his own people. Why might Mark end the story there instead of with him leaving in the boat?

lessons.title: Three Rebellions, Three Groups
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser sorted the Bible's dark powers into three groups, each tied to one rebellion in Genesis.
reading: Many people use the words Satan, fallen angels and demons as if they meant the same thing. Michael Heiser thought the Bible tells a more careful story. In The Unseen Realm (2015) and Demons (2020), he traced three *rebellions* in Genesis. He argued that each one explains a different group of dark powers.

The first rebellion is in Eden, Genesis 3. There the serpent turns humans away from God. Heiser saw this rebel as the one the New Testament calls Satan and the devil. The second is Genesis 6:1–4, where the sons of God take human wives and the Nephilim, or giants, are born. The third is Babel, Genesis 11, when God scatters the nations.

From these, Heiser drew three groups. First, the Eden rebel, the devil. Second, the sons of God set over the nations after Babel, who became corrupt. Paul's letters call powers like these *principalities*, or rulers. Third, demons: in Heiser's reading, the spirits of the dead giants.
Not every scholar sorts things this way. Many Christian teachers treat all these as one group of fallen angels led by Satan. But Heiser's three groups give a map for the rest of this chapter.

words.d: acts of rising up against a rightful ruler; Heiser found three in Genesis 3, 6 and 11
an older English word for rulers; in Paul's letters, spiritual powers over the world
evil spirits; the Gospels also call them unclean spirits

look.title: Heiser's Map
look.text: Genesis 3, Eden: the serpent rebels. Group: the devil, or Satan. Genesis 6, the sons of God and the giants: Group: demons, the giants' spirits. Genesis 11, Babel: the nations are scattered under other sons of God. Group: principalities, the rulers over nations.
look.prompt: Explain Heiser's map in your own words. Which rebellion goes with which group, and why?

check.q: Which three chapters of Genesis did Heiser connect to three rebellions?
check.why: Heiser traced rebellions in Eden (Genesis 3), with the sons of God (Genesis 6) and at Babel (Genesis 11).

check.q: In Heiser's reading, what are demons?
choices: The spirits of the dead giants
The rulers set over the nations
check.why: Heiser read demons as the spirits of the giants, the Nephilim, born in the Genesis 6 story.

check.q: How do many Christian teachers group these powers differently from Heiser?
choices: As one group of fallen angels led by Satan
As three kinds of human kings
As powers that appear only in Job
As spirits named in the Septuagint only
check.why: Many Christian teachers treat all dark powers as fallen angels led by Satan, rather than Heiser's three groups.

lessons.title: Rulers Over the Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser linked Paul's principalities and powers to the sons of God who were set over the nations and turned from God.
reading: Deuteronomy 32:8, in the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint, says God divided the nations by the number of the sons of God. Heiser read this to mean God placed the nations under lesser heavenly beings. Israel stayed God's own portion. You met this reading in the unit on the gods of the nations.

A few verses later, Deuteronomy 32:17 says Israel sacrificed to *shedim*, not to God. Shedim is a Hebrew word for spirit beings. It is related to a word in Akkadian, the language of ancient Mesopotamia. The Greek Septuagint translated it daimonia, demons. The KJV says "devils".

Daniel 10 speaks of a prince of Persia and a prince of Greece who resist a heavenly messenger. Paul, writing in Greek, uses words like rulers, authorities and powers. Ephesians 6:12 says the struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers of darkness in the heavenly places.

Heiser argued these rulers are the sons of God of Deuteronomy 32, who turned corrupt, as Psalm 82 describes. In his reading they are not demons in the Gospel sense. They are higher powers tied to nations and places. Other scholars read Paul's powers as human and social systems, or as all spirits together.

words.d: a Hebrew word for spirit beings, used in Deuteronomy 32:17; the Septuagint translated it demons
in Paul's letters, a word for spiritual rulers or authorities

look.title: Sacrifices to Shedim
look.text: They sacrificed unto devils, not to God; to gods whom they knew not, to new gods that came newly up, whom your fathers feared not.
look.prompt: The KJV word "devils" translates the Hebrew shedim. How does the verse describe these beings? What does it say they are not?

check.q: What Hebrew word in Deuteronomy 32:17 names the spirit beings Israel sacrificed to?
check.why: Deuteronomy 32:17 uses shedim. The Septuagint translated it daimonia, and the KJV says devils.

check.q: Which verse says the struggle is against rulers and powers, not flesh and blood?
check.why: Ephesians 6:12 says the struggle is against rulers and powers of darkness in the heavenly places.

check.q: Who did Heiser think Paul's rulers and powers were?
choices: The corrupt sons of God set over the nations
The spirits of the dead giants
check.why: Heiser linked Paul's rulers and powers to the sons of God of Deuteronomy 32 who turned corrupt. Demons were a separate group.

lessons.title: Unclean Spirits
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels call demons unclean spirits, using a word from Israel's laws about what may come near God's holy presence.
reading: The Gospel of Mark often uses the phrase *unclean spirit*. In Greek it is pneuma akatharton. Mark also uses daimonion, *demon*, for the same beings. The KJV usually translates daimonion as "devil", so it can say Jesus cast out many devils. Modern translations usually say demons.

Why unclean? In the Law of Moses, being unclean did not mean being dirty or bad. It meant not being ready to come near God's holy presence. Touching a dead body made a person unclean for a time, as Numbers 19 says. Certain animals, like pigs, were unclean to eat. There were ways to become clean again.

Scholars have noticed how many unclean things fill the story of the man from the tombs. The tombs held the dead. The land was outside Israel. A herd of pigs fed nearby. In that setting, Mark says an unclean spirit troubled the man, and Jesus set him free.
So the name tells readers something. In the Gospels, these spirits stand against God's holy presence. Jesus, in the stories, has authority over them.

words.d: the Gospels' phrase for a demon; unclean means not fit to come near God's holy presence
from the Greek daimonion; an evil spirit in the New Testament, often called "devil" in the KJV

look.title: Clean and Unclean
look.text: In the Law of Moses, a person who touched a dead body was unclean for seven days and then washed to become clean again (Numbers 19:11–12). Pigs were unclean animals to eat (Leviticus 11:7). In Mark 5, a man lives among tombs, in a land outside Israel, near a herd of pigs.
look.prompt: Why might Mark's first readers notice the unclean things in this setting? What does the story show Jesus doing in that place?

check.q: In the Law of Moses, what did "unclean" mean?
choices: Not ready to come near God's holy presence
check.why: Unclean meant not fit to come near God's holy presence for a time. Laws such as Numbers 19 showed how to become clean again.

check.q: How does the KJV usually translate the Greek daimonion?
check.why: The KJV usually renders daimonion as devil, as in cast out many devils. Modern translations usually say demon.

check.q: Which detail from Mark 5 is NOT one of the unclean things in the setting?
check.why: The tombs, the pigs and the land outside Israel were all unclean under the Law. The boat was not.

lessons.title: What 1 Enoch 15 Says
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch 15 says that when the giants died, their spirits went out as evil spirits on the earth.
reading: *1 Enoch* is an ancient Jewish book, written in parts between about 300 BCE and the time of Jesus. Pieces of it in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. The full book survives in Ge'ez, the old language of Ethiopia. It is part of the Bible only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

Its first part, the Book of the *Watchers*, retells Genesis 6. In 1 Enoch, the Watchers are heavenly beings who came down to earth, took human wives and fathered giants. The giants brought violence, and God sent judgment. In chapters 12–16, the Watchers ask Enoch to plead for them, and God gives Enoch a reply.

In 1 Enoch 15:8–12, God explains what happens to the giants. They were born from spirits and flesh. So when their bodies die, the spirits that come out of them will be called evil spirits on the earth. The earth will be their home. They will trouble people, because they came from people.
This is one of the earliest explanations of evil spirits that survives. It appears in a Jewish book that many people read in the centuries before the Gospels were written.

words.d: an ancient Jewish book about Enoch and the Watchers, canonical in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
in 1 Enoch, heavenly beings who came down, took human wives and fathered giants

look.title: The Giants' Spirits
look.text: The giants were born from spirits and from flesh. So they will be called evil spirits upon the earth, and the earth will be where they live. Evil spirits have come out of their bodies.
look.cite: 1 Enoch 15:8–9, after R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917) (paraphrased)
look.prompt: According to this passage, why do the giants' spirits stay on the earth instead of going to heaven?

check.q: According to 1 Enoch 15, what happens when the giants' bodies die?
choices: Their spirits become evil spirits on the earth
They rise to heaven as angels
They become stars in the sky
They turn into the Rephaim kings
check.why: 1 Enoch 15:8–9 says the spirits that come out of the giants will be called evil spirits and will live on the earth.

check.q: Which churches include 1 Enoch in their Bible?
choices: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
check.why: 1 Enoch is canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

check.q: Who asks Enoch to plead for them in 1 Enoch 12–16?
check.why: In 1 Enoch the Watchers ask Enoch to plead with God for them, and God sends back a reply of judgment.

lessons.title: Heiser's Case
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that 1 Enoch's giant spirits are where Jewish readers of Jesus's day got their idea of unclean spirits.
reading: The Hebrew Bible says little about demons like those in the Gospels. Then, in the Gospels, unclean spirits appear often. Heiser asked where this idea came from. In Reversing Hermon (2017) and Demons (2020), he pointed to 1 Enoch 15.

His case had three steps. First, 1 Enoch was widely read by Jews in the *Second Temple* period; the Dead Sea Scrolls contain several copies of it. Second, 1 Enoch explains evil spirits as the spirits of dead giants who remain on the earth. Third, the New Testament shows that its writers knew 1 Enoch. Jude 14–15 quotes it by name.

So, Heiser argued, when Gospel readers heard of unclean spirits, many would have thought of the giants' spirits. Some readers also see a reason for the word unclean. The giants were a mix of heavenly and earthly, and the Law's ideas of holiness kept such things apart.

Heiser offered this as the best explanation of the evidence, not as the only possible one. The Gospels themselves never say where demons come from. His case rests on reading them alongside the Jewish books their first readers knew.

words.d: the period from about 516 BCE to 70 CE, when Jerusalem's second temple stood
facts or texts that support an argument

look.title: The Five Parts of 1 Enoch
look.cite: The standard five-part division of 1 Enoch, as in R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917)
look.prompt: Chapter 15 falls in which part? Which part is the longest, and which is the shortest?

check.q: Which New Testament book quotes 1 Enoch by name?
check.why: Jude 14–15 quotes a prophecy of Enoch, which matches 1 Enoch 1:9.

check.q: Which step is part of Heiser's case?
choices: 1 Enoch was widely read, and copies were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls
The Gospels say plainly where demons come from
Leviticus names the giants as demons
check.why: Heiser pointed out that 1 Enoch was widely read, as copies among the Dead Sea Scrolls show. The Gospels themselves do not give an origin.

check.q: In which part of 1 Enoch is chapter 15?
check.why: The Book of the Watchers covers chapters 1–36, so chapter 15 is in it.

lessons.title: Other Answers
lessons.mainIdea: Many Christians have taught that demons are fallen angels, while other ancient writers held views close to 1 Enoch's.
reading: A common Christian view says demons are *fallen angels* themselves. On this view, when Satan rebelled, some angels joined him. Readers point to Revelation 12:9, which says the dragon's angels were thrown down with him. Matthew 25:41 also speaks of the devil and his angels.

Other early Christians held views close to 1 Enoch's. Justin Martyr, a Christian writer around 150 CE, wrote that angels fathered children with women, and that these children are the ones called demons. So Heiser's reading has ancient company.

Jewish writings give still more accounts. The book of *Jubilees*, from about 160 BCE, tells of evil spirits that trouble Noah's grandchildren. God binds nine-tenths of them and leaves one-tenth under Mastema. Later rabbis wrote about spirits in many different ways.

Heiser argued in Demons (2020) that the Bible's dark powers are not all one kind of being. Other scholars reply that the texts do not settle the question. Readers can weigh each view by the passages it uses.

words.d: angels who, in many Christian teachings, joined Satan's rebellion against God
a Jewish book from about 160 BCE that retells Genesis and early Exodus

look.title: Two Views, Two Kinds of Evidence
look.text: View 1: Demons are fallen angels who followed Satan. Key texts: Revelation 12:9; Matthew 25:41. View 2 (Heiser and 1 Enoch): Demons are the spirits of the dead giants. Key texts: Genesis 6:1–4; 1 Enoch 15:8–12; also Justin Martyr, about 150 CE.
look.prompt: What kind of source does each view lean on most? What would you want to read next to test either view?

check.q: Which verse do readers use to say demons are fallen angels?
choices: Revelation 12:9, where the dragon's angels are thrown down
check.why: Revelation 12:9 says the dragon's angels were thrown down with him, which supports the fallen-angel view.

check.q: Which early Christian writer said demons were the children of angels and women?
check.why: Justin Martyr, around 150 CE, wrote that angels fathered children with women and those children are called demons.

check.q: In Jubilees, how many of the evil spirits are left under Mastema?
check.why: In Jubilees 10 God binds nine-tenths of the spirits and leaves one-tenth under Mastema.

lessons.title: In the Synagogue at Capernaum
lessons.mainIdea: Mark's first story of Jesus's work shows him freeing a man from an unclean spirit with a word, and the crowd amazed at his authority.
reading: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee. Mark 1:21–28 says Jesus taught there in the *synagogue*, a Jewish meeting place for prayer and study, on the Sabbath. The people were amazed. He taught with authority, not like the scribes.

Then a man with an unclean spirit cried out. The spirit asked what Jesus wanted with them, and called him the Holy One of God. Jesus told it to be silent and come out. Mark says the spirit shook the man, cried out and left him.

The crowd's question is the point of the story. They asked what this new teaching was, since even unclean spirits obeyed him. News about Jesus spread through all of Galilee. Mark puts this story near the start of his Gospel. It sets up Jesus's *authority* as a main theme.

Heiser read these stories as part of a larger picture. In his view, Jesus came to take back what the dark powers had claimed. Other readers focus on what the story shows about Jesus's teaching or about the man. All agree that Mark wants readers to ask who Jesus is.

words.d: a Jewish meeting place for prayer, reading and study
the right and power to give commands that others obey

look.title: The Crowd Wonders
look.text: What thing is this? what new doctrine is this? for with authority commandeth he even the unclean spirits, and they do obey him.
look.prompt: What two things amaze the crowd? Why might Mark place their question at the very start of his Gospel?

check.q: Where does the story in Mark 1:21–28 take place?
choices: Among the tombs of the Gerasenes
check.why: Mark 1:21 says Jesus taught in the synagogue at Capernaum on the Sabbath.

check.q: What amazed the crowd in Mark 1:27?
choices: Even unclean spirits obeyed Jesus's word
Jesus sailed across the sea at night
check.why: The crowd asked what this new teaching was, since Jesus commanded even unclean spirits with authority.

check.q: What does the unclean spirit call Jesus?
check.why: In Mark 1:24 the spirit calls Jesus the Holy One of God.

lessons.title: The Man from the Tombs
lessons.mainIdea: In Mark 5 Jesus frees a man near the tombs and sends him home to his own people to tell his story.
reading: Mark 5:1–20 is set in the country of the Gerasenes, east of the Sea of Galilee. A man lived among the tombs, apart from his town. When he saw Jesus, he ran and knelt before him. Jesus asked the spirit's name. It answered *Legion*, the word for a Roman army unit of thousands, "for we are many."

The spirits asked to be sent into a herd of pigs on the hillside. Jesus allowed it. Mark says about two thousand pigs rushed down the steep bank into the sea. The herders ran to tell the town. When people came, they found the man sitting with Jesus, dressed and calm.

The townspeople were afraid and asked Jesus to leave. The man begged to go with him. Jesus said no. He sent the man home to his friends, to tell them what the Lord had done and how he had shown him mercy. The man told his story in the *Decapolis*, the Ten Cities, and people were amazed.
The story ends with a person back among his people. He has a home, friends and a town. Instead of being avoided, he is the one telling the news.

words.d: a Roman army unit of several thousand soldiers; the name the spirit gives in Mark 5:9
Greek for Ten Cities; a group of mostly non-Jewish towns east of the Sea of Galilee

look.title: Go Home
look.text: Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.
look.prompt: "Suffered him not" means "did not let him". What does Jesus not let the man do, and what does he send him to do instead?

check.q: What does the name Legion refer to?
choices: A Roman army unit of thousands
A town in the Ten Cities
A book of the Dead Sea Scrolls
check.why: A legion was a Roman army unit of several thousand, which fits the answer "for we are many" in Mark 5:9.

check.q: What did Jesus tell the man to do in Mark 5:19?
choices: Go home to his friends and tell them what the Lord had done
Get into the boat and follow him
Stay among the tombs and wait
Travel to Jerusalem to see the priests
check.why: Mark 5:19 says Jesus sent him home to his friends to tell how the Lord had shown him mercy.

check.q: Where did the man tell his story?
choices: In the Decapolis, the Ten Cities
In the court of the king of Tyre
check.why: Mark 5:20 says he told what Jesus had done for him throughout the Decapolis.

lessons.title: Reading These Stories With Care
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels treat healing the sick and freeing people from spirits as different things, and they end these stories with people restored to their communities.
reading: Read Mark 1:32–34 closely. At sunset, people bring to Jesus those who were sick and those troubled by demons. Mark then says he healed many who were sick with various diseases and cast out many demons. Mark lists these as two separate groups. Matthew 4:24 does the same.

This matters for how the stories are read today. Illness, disability and differences in how people's minds work are a normal part of human life. They are never a sign of an evil spirit, and no one should ever be treated that way. The Gospel writers themselves kept healing and freeing apart.

Look also at how the stories end. The man in Capernaum is freed right in his own town's synagogue. The man from the tombs goes home to his friends. In Mark 5:34 a woman who is healed is called daughter. The people in these stories have names, homes and families. The stories end with *restoration*: a person welcomed back.
This course studies how these texts were read. It does not teach any spiritual practice. Readers from many backgrounds notice two things in these stories: Jesus's authority and his care for people.

words.d: bringing someone or something back to a good and whole state
a group of people who live together and belong to one another

look.title: Two Groups in One Verse
look.text: Paraphrase of Mark 1:32–34: That evening, after sunset, people brought to Jesus all who were sick and all who were troubled by demons. The whole town gathered at the door. He healed many who had various diseases, and he cast out many demons.
look.prompt: How many different groups of people does this passage name? What does that tell you about how Mark saw sickness and spirits?

check.q: How does Mark 1:32–34 describe the people brought to Jesus?
choices: As two separate groups: the sick and those troubled by demons
As one group, all troubled by spirits
As soldiers from a Roman legion
check.why: Mark 1:32–34 names the sick and those troubled by demons as two groups, and says Jesus healed one and cast out the other.

check.q: How do the Gospel stories of freeing people usually end?
choices: With the person restored to home and community
With the person sent away from town
With the person hidden in the tombs
With the person forgotten by the writer
check.why: The stories end in restoration: the man from the tombs, for example, goes home to tell his friends.

check.q: Which statement fits how these stories should be read today?
choices: Illness, disability and different minds are never signs of an evil spirit
Healing and freeing mean the same thing in Mark
Matthew joins sickness and spirits into one group
The Gospels give steps for readers to follow
check.why: The Gospels keep healing and freeing apart, and illness, disability and different minds are part of human life, never a spirit.

sections.title: Azazel and the Day of Atonement

lessons.title: Two Goats
lessons.mainIdea: On the Day of Atonement, one goat was offered to the LORD and the other carried the people's sins into the wilderness, for Azazel.
reading: Leviticus 16 describes the *Day of Atonement*, Yom Kippur. Once a year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, the high priest entered the Most Holy Place. The day was set aside to make the people and the sanctuary clean before God. Jews still keep Yom Kippur today as a day of fasting and prayer.

The ceremony used two goats. The high priest cast lots over them. One lot was for the LORD, and the other was for *Azazel*. The goat for the LORD was offered as a sin offering. Its blood was used to cleanse the sanctuary.

Then the high priest laid both hands on the head of the living goat. He confessed over it all the sins of the people. A man led the goat away into the wilderness. Leviticus 16:22 says the goat carried the people's sins to a land cut off from people.

The picture is clear even to a first-time reader. The people's wrongs are not just forgiven. They are carried away, far from the camp, out of sight. Readers have long asked the same question: who or what is Azazel?

words.d: Yom Kippur, the yearly day in Leviticus 16 for cleansing the people and the sanctuary
the name in Leviticus 16:8 to which the second goat is sent; its meaning is debated

look.title: Leviticus 16 by the Numbers
rows: Rams (one for Aaron, one for the people)
look.prompt: Of the two goats, how many were offered on the altar? What happened to the other one?

check.q: What did the high priest do with the living goat before it was sent away?
choices: Laid his hands on it and confessed the people's sins
check.why: Leviticus 16:21 says he laid both hands on the living goat and confessed all the people's sins over it.

check.q: How were the two goats assigned?
choices: By casting lots, one for the LORD and one for Azazel
By age, the older one for Azazel
By color, the dark one for the LORD
check.why: Leviticus 16:8 says the high priest cast lots over the two goats: one for the LORD and one for Azazel.

check.q: When did the Day of Atonement fall?
choices: On the tenth day of the seventh month
On the first day of the first month
On the day of a new king
check.why: Leviticus 16:29 sets it on the tenth day of the seventh month, once a year.

lessons.title: Who Is Azazel?
lessons.mainIdea: Azazel has been read as a wilderness spirit, as the goat that goes away, and as a rugged place; Heiser linked it to the Azazel of 1 Enoch.
reading: In 1530 the English translator William Tyndale read Azazel as "the goat that goes away" and made up a new word: *scapegoat*. The King James Version kept it. Today scapegoat means someone blamed for others' wrongs. Some readers still favor a reading close to Tyndale's.

Some later rabbis read Azazel as the name of a place: a rough, steep cliff in the wilderness. The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, describes the goat being taken to a high rocky place. On this reading, Azazel names where the goat went.

1 Enoch gives Azazel a different role. In 1 Enoch 8, Azazel is one of the leaders of the Watchers. He taught people to make weapons and jewelry. In 1 Enoch 10:4–5, God tells the angel Raphael to bind Azazel and cast him into darkness in the desert, under rough, jagged rocks.

Heiser read Azazel as a wilderness *spirit being*, as 1 Enoch does. But he stressed that the goat was not a gift to Azazel. In his reading, it carried the people's sins out of the holy camp. It sent them back to the wild place linked with evil, away from God's presence.

words.d: Tyndale's 1530 word for the goat sent away in Leviticus 16; now someone blamed for others' wrongs
a being of the unseen world, such as an angel, rather than a human or animal

look.title: Azazel Bound
look.text: The Lord told Raphael to bind Azazel hand and foot and throw him into the darkness. Raphael was to make an opening in the desert and put him there, and to lay rough, jagged rocks over him.
look.cite: 1 Enoch 10:4–5, after R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917) (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Leviticus 16 sends a goat into the wilderness, and 1 Enoch binds Azazel in the desert. Why might Heiser see a link between the two?

check.q: Who coined the English word scapegoat?
check.why: William Tyndale made up scapegoat in 1530 for the goat that goes away. The KJV kept his word.

check.q: In 1 Enoch 10, what happens to Azazel?
choices: Raphael binds him and casts him into darkness in the desert
He becomes high priest of Israel
He is sent to rule Babylon
He is forgiven and made a cherub
check.why: 1 Enoch 10:4–5 says Raphael binds Azazel and casts him into darkness in the desert under jagged rocks.

check.q: How did Heiser read the goat for Azazel?
choices: It carried sins away to the wild place linked with evil, not as a gift to Azazel
It was an offering to please Azazel
It was a name for a rocky cliff only
It was a symbol of the king of Tyre
check.why: Heiser read Azazel as a wilderness spirit, but said the goat was not offered to him. It removed the people's sins from the holy camp.

review.q: In Heiser's three groups, which one comes from the Babel story?
review.why: Heiser tied the rulers, or principalities, to the sons of God set over the scattered nations after Babel.

review.q: Which ancient book says the giants' spirits became evil spirits on the earth?
review.why: 1 Enoch 15:8–12 says the spirits that came out of the dead giants became evil spirits living on the earth.

review.q: What did Heiser argue about 1 Enoch 15?
choices: It is where Jewish readers of Jesus's day got their idea of unclean spirits
It was written after the Gospels
It is part of every Protestant Bible
It describes the Day of Atonement
review.why: Heiser argued that 1 Enoch, widely read in the Second Temple period, shaped how Gospel readers understood unclean spirits.

review.q: What does the common Christian view say demons are?
review.why: Many Christians teach that demons are angels who joined Satan's rebellion, citing Revelation 12:9 and Matthew 25:41.

review.q: What happens at the end of the story of the man from the tombs?
choices: He goes home and tells his story in the Ten Cities
He sails away with Jesus to Capernaum
He is sent into the wilderness like the goat
He becomes a priest in Jerusalem
review.why: In Mark 5:19–20 Jesus sends him home, and he tells what the Lord did for him in the Decapolis.

review.q: Why does Mark 1:32–34 matter for reading these stories with care?
choices: It lists the sick and those troubled by demons as separate groups
It says Jesus stayed away from the town
It gives steps for casting out spirits
It names the giants of Genesis 6
review.why: Mark 1:32–34 names the sick and the troubled as two groups, keeping healing and freeing apart.

review.q: Which reading of Azazel comes from the Talmud?
choices: A rough, steep place in the wilderness
review.why: Tractate Yoma in the Talmud reads Azazel as a rocky place. 1 Enoch makes Azazel a Watcher, and Tyndale read it as the goat that goes away.

review.q: What Greek word gives the New Testament word demon?
review.why: Demon comes from daimonion. Diabolos gives devil, Satanas is Satan, and pneuma means spirit.
